title: Sound Grammar: The Best Jazz Records of 2026, So Far
author: Jeffrey St. Clair
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/07/midyearjazz-680x435.png)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/07/29/sound-
grammar-the-best-jazz-records-of-2026-so-far/)
![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/07/midyearjazz-680x435.png)

If you want to discover how people feel about the way the world is going,
don’t look to language to tell you, not to articles like this one, or even
those of the most informed and articulate. I’ve run out of words to say. But
keep using them, which makes the words even more impotent. Language always
fails. It can’t express the inexpressible and when it tries to do so, language
leads us astray, into wrong turns and cul-de-sacs that are hard to find our
way out of. As Bill Evans said, “Words are the children of reason and,
therefore, can't explain it. They really can't translate feeling because
they're not part of it.” What doesn’t lead us astray is music, especially
improvised music, played in the moment, as a true expression of feeling in
real time.

The act of listening to “jazz,” for lack of a better word, can be just as
improvisational as the music itself. The music doesn’t instruct you how you
should feel about the feelings it expresses or how you should respond to it.
In that sense, it’s liberated from the restrictions imposed by language. And
those impressions, to use Coltrane’s word, almost certainly change over time;
they become new again with each new hearing. For Charles Mingus “Jazz is, or
was, a language of the emotions." True, but it’s also a language of the
intellect, and there were few deeper intellects than Mingus, played out in
notes and chords and progressions and changes and spaces. Often, the key is to
be found in the negative spaces of the music.

Jazz is a word that doesn’t fully capture the music we call “jazz.” Many of
the black musicians who played music marketed as “jazz” in the 60s,
especially, refused to use the term. I understand what they were getting at,
beyond the implied racism of the word. The title of Gaudi’s "Jazz Gone Dub"
highlights the contradiction and then the music tears it asunder. How can Monk
still speak to us with urgency seven decades later? Because the Monk we’re
hearing has been transported across time and place and cultures to the now by
the way Ahmed feels and plays the music. So Ahmed’s recording isn’t a retreat
to the past but an assertion into the future. Monk’s music defies stasis and
gains new immediacy through Ahmed’s playing.

Even Monk's own live recording from a 1959 solo gig in San Francisco's Fugazi
Hall sounds current, played in the moment, as in the improvised blues of
"[Round Lights](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8ZGXb2AcExM)" and
"[Bluehawk.](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Lr85cOPdcNE)" Unlike language,
Monk claimed that "the piano ain't got any wrong notes." There’s nothing to
mediate between you and the notes. Nothing to mislead you as to its meaning.
The meaning is buried in how you experience it and how you feel about it. And
how you hear “[Pannonica](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aSLpyw1Kvms)” today
won’t be the way you hear it next week and the way Monk played it on this
night in San Francisco won’t be the same way he played it before or ever
again.

Music therefore can reach us without conditions, without expectations or
contrived limits. It seeps through the boundaries of accepted discourse and
hits us in the gut and the head and heart at the same time. And can only
dispute the message if you play the sax, which has rarely, if ever, been an
instrument of fascism. Jazz has other advantages in times of autocracy. It can
express radical, even revolutionary, ideas and sentiments without falling
under the censor’s lash. Bill Orcutt’s Music in Continuous Time may well be a
call for sedition against the regime, but good luck to Todd Blanche proving it
or even understanding it.

So in that spirit of subversion, I offer here my Francis Davis Jazz Critics
Mid-Year Poll ballot for the best new jazz and reissues so far in the
enervating year of 2026. The full results from more than 120 other music
writers can be found on [Tom Hull’s
site](https://hullworks.net/jazzpoll/26my/), which is essential reading for
music fans, and on [Arts Fuse](https://artsfuse.org/331941/the-annual-francis-
davis-jazz-critics-poll-at-mid-year-warming-up-a-riff-how-it-happened-and-why-
it-matters/).
